03 — Branding · Web · E-commerce

Ice Cream Solutions: letting packaging colour do the navigation's job.

A website for a four-flavour popsicle line, where each flavour's packaging colour becomes the background of its own navigation state — so the site feels like the product, not a template wrapped around it.

RoleUI/UX & Visual Designer (solo)
PlatformWeb — desktop & responsive
ToolsFigma
Timelineadd duration
Overview

Four flavours, four navigation states

Ice Cream Solutions sells four popsicle flavours — Lime, Pineapple, Grape, Strawberry. The site's core idea: the top navigation bar is split into four colour blocks, one per flavour, matching each product's actual packaging illustration. Hover or land on a section and that flavour's colour and hero photograph take over the page.

Problem

A four-product catalogue that still needs a strong identity

Small product ranges are easy to under-design — four items don't obviously need a rich navigation system. The risk was a generic single-colour site with four thumbnail cards. The brief I set myself was to make the range itself the design system, so browsing the site feels like the same pleasure as choosing a flavour off a shelf.

Users
  • First-time visitors deciding which flavour to try, comparing packaging and description before buying.
  • Returning customers who already know their flavour and want the fastest path to that product's page.
Research

Studying the packaging before touching the layout

I started from the four packaging illustrations rather than a moodboard — each design already has a strong colour and pattern language (Lime's citrus green, Pineapple's dark gold, Grape's violet, Strawberry's pink-and-floral). The site's job became translating that existing brand language into a navigable structure, not inventing a new one on top of it.

Competitive analysis

Pattern seen

Most small food-brand sites use one accent colour across every page, regardless of which product is being shown.

Design response

The whole page — nav, hero photo, background — recolours per flavour. Colour becomes the wayfinding system instead of a fixed brand rule.

Persona
R

Rafi, 19 — browsing on his phone before a summer order

Goal: quickly see which flavour looks best before ordering for a group.
Frustration: product sites that make every item look the same at a glance.
What he needs: a fast visual read on each flavour's personality, not just a name and a price.

Information architecture

Home / About Us / Ice Cream / Category / Contact Us / Sign In — a flat six-item nav, with "Ice Cream" and "Category" doing the heavy lifting (product range and flavour-type filtering respectively). The four-flavour colour system sits underneath this same nav bar rather than replacing it, so wayfinding stays predictable even as the colour shifts.

User flow

Landing page shows all four flavour blocks side by side as an entry menu → visitor clicks (or on desktop, hovers) a flavour → that flavour's colour, hero photograph, and packaging shot expand to fill the page → an arrow prompt invites the visitor further into that product's detail. The arrow icon repeats in every state, so it reads as a consistent "go deeper" affordance rather than a one-off decoration.

Wireframes

Testing the split-nav concept first

Before any photography went in, I wireframed the four-way colour split as plain rectangles to confirm the proportions worked at both a wide desktop viewport and a narrower one — the split needed to stay legible even when compressed.

Design process & UI decisions

Letting the product photography lead

Each flavour state pairs its packaging illustration with a real photograph of the popsicle itself — the illustration sells the brand, the photograph sells the appetite. Typography stays a plain, confident serif logotype-style wordmark per flavour, kept large enough to double as a poster if the brand ever needed print collateral.

Challenges

Four strong, distinct colours risk clashing the instant they appear on screen together in the resting nav state. I resolved this by keeping the resting state to flat colour blocks with no gradients, and reserving photography and pattern detail for the expanded/active state only — busy detail earns its place once a flavour is chosen, not before.

Outcome
4Flavour states designed
6Navigation destinations
— add —Click-through rate per flavour, if tested
Reflection

This was the project where I trusted existing brand assets the most instead of designing a system from zero — and it worked better for it. It's a useful reminder that "distinctive design" often means listening closely to what's already there, not adding more.

Next improvements
  • Design the actual product/cart pages behind "Category" and "Sign In," currently out of scope.
  • Test whether the four-colour nav still reads clearly for colour-blind visitors, and add a text label fallback if not.
  • Extend the system to a fifth flavour to confirm the layout scales past four.
